title: Those Who Coach Others Are More Receptive to Feedback
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that assigning team members short-term coaching roles for their peers produces a valuable secondary benefit beyond skill development: those who coach others become more receptive to being coached themselves. It describes a peer-coaching model where colleagues rotate through brief mentoring assignments, including reverse mentoring where juniors help seniors, and notes this builds both leadership skill and deeper team relationships. The piece frames peer coaching as a way to distribute development responsibility across the whole team rather than relying solely on the formal leader.
points: Assigning team members short-term coaching roles for peers has a secondary benefit: coaches become more receptive to feedback themselves.
Being on the "supply side" of feedback changes how people relate to and value criticism.
Peer-coaching assignments should be brief and rotating, including reverse mentoring where juniors coach seniors.
High-performing teams typically have most members having recently completed a peer coaching assignment.
Peer coaching builds both individual leadership skill and deeper relationships across the team.
quotes: Developing the talents, skills, and knowledge of team members is not a solo act for team leaders.
They quickly learn that those who coach others are more receptive to the coaching efforts of the leader.
By serving in the role of coach for a colleague, they naturally reevaluate the purpose of criticism and how important it is for improving performance.
Leaders constantly dole out these assignments, making sure not to overlook the possibility of reverse mentoring where juniors assist seniors in areas of their know-how and strength.
Peers coaching peers unleashes a learning and performance mindset in a more powerful way than any one leader could achieve on their own.
